summary: This Wikipedia-derived note surveys the crucifixion of Jesus, covering its historical certainty among scholars, the Marian presence at the cross in art and devotion, debates over the day and time of the crucifixion, and the number of nails used. It also covers Pauline and later theological interpretations, archaeological finds such as the body of Yehohanan ben Hagkol, a combined Gospel account of the trial and events leading to the crucifixion, early non-Christian references, and Frederick Zugibe's forensic experiments.
one_line: Overview of the crucifixion of Jesus covering its historical certainty, timing debates, nails, theology, archaeology, and forensic analysis.
key_facts: James Dunn states that the baptism of Jesus and his crucifixion 'rank so high on the almost impossible to doubt or deny scale of historical facts'.
Bart Ehrman states that the crucifixion of Jesus on the orders of Pontius Pilate is the most certain element about him.
John Dominic Crossan states that the crucifixion of Jesus is as certain as any historical fact can be.
The consensus of modern scholarship is that the New Testament accounts represent a crucifixion occurring on a Friday, though a Thursday or Wednesday crucifixion have also been proposed.
Mark 15:25 places the crucifixion at the third hour (9 a.m.) and Jesus' death at the ninth hour (3 p.m.), while John 19:14 has Jesus still before Pilate at the sixth hour.
Theories about the number of nails in the crucifixion suggest three or four nails, and at times as many as 14 nails have been hypothesized.
In the Western Church before the Renaissance, usually four nails were depicted, with the feet side by side; after the Renaissance most depictions use three nails.
The 1968 archaeological discovery northeast of Jerusalem of a crucified man's body dated to the 1st century provided confirmatory evidence of Roman-period crucifixion.
The crucified man was identified as Yehohanan ben Hagkol and probably died about 70 AD, around the time of the Jewish revolt against Rome.
The analyses at the Hadassah Medical School estimated that Yehohanan ben Hagkol died in his late 20s.
Paul's Christology focuses on the death and resurrection of Jesus, and the term 'the cross of Christ' in Galatians 6:12 may be viewed as his abbreviation of the gospel message.
For Paul, the crucifixion of Jesus was a cosmic event with significant eschatological consequences, as in 1 Corinthians 2:8.
John Calvin argued that Jesus could have successfully argued for his innocence in Pilate's court but instead submitted to crucifixion in obedience to the Father.
Sergei Bulgakov argued that the crucifixion was 'pre-eternally' determined by the Father before the creation of the world to redeem humanity from the disgrace caused by the fall of Adam.
Mara Bar-Serapion's letter to his son, written sometime after AD 73 but before the 3rd century AD, is likely an early non-Christian reference to the crucifixion of Jesus.

Frederick Zugibe, a physician and forensic pathologist, studied the likely circumstances of Jesus' death in his book The Crucifixion of Jesus, using experiments with volunteers hanging at specific angles.
